messages.content: I need a design for distributed garbage collection that safely reclaims cycles even with concurrent object migration, network partitions, and crash recovery. The safety requirement is strict: never reclaim an object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference during crashes, partitions, or migration. The progress requirement is to reclaim unreachable cycles within 3 collection rounds after recovery and quiescence, without global pauses.

That calls for two guarantees. Safety must hold throughout failures and migration: incomplete information must never cause the collector to treat an object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference as garbage. Progress is conditional: once recovery and quiescence have occurred, an unreachable cycle must be reclaimed within 3 collection rounds, without globally pausing the system. The design has to satisfy both; merely retaining everything would be safe but would not meet the progress requirement.
Why emphasize in-flight references separately from durable roots?

A durable root and an in-flight reference are different ways an object can remain reachable. In particular, a reference being transferred must not disappear from the collector’s account simply because it is not presently represented at an endpoint the collector can inspect. The requirement protects objects reachable through either source, including while crashes, partitions, or migration complicate observation.
So if a message carrying a reference is delayed by a partition, the collector cannot infer that its target is garbage?

Right. A partition or delay is not proof that the reference has ceased to exist. Reclaiming its target on that basis could violate the never-reclaim guarantee. The design needs to remain conservative where it lacks the evidence needed for safe reclamation.
Does that mean the collector can simply wait out every partition?

The stated bound begins after recovery and quiescence, so it does not require reclamation within 3 rounds while a partition is still preventing recovery. Waiting under uncertainty can protect safety, but waiting indefinitely after recovery and quiescence would not satisfy the progress requirement for an unreachable cycle.
How does concurrent migration affect the same issue?

Migration changes where an object is represented while collection may be examining reachability. The object must not be judged unreachable merely because observations made during that movement are incomplete. At the same time, migration cannot leave genuinely unreachable cycles unreclaimed beyond the stated post-recovery, post-quiescence bound.
And a crash cannot turn a temporarily missing reference into evidence of unreachability?

Exactly. Safety must survive crashes and crash recovery. If an object remains reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference, a crash-related gap in what the collector can observe must not result in its reclamation.
What does reclaiming cycles add to the goal? Isn't ordinary reachability enough?

The goal expressly includes unreachable cycles. Objects in a cycle can still refer to one another even when no protected path reaches the cycle. Those internal references must not, by themselves, prevent reclamation once the cycle is unreachable. Conversely, if a durable root or an in-flight reference reaches any part of it, the collector must not reclaim reachable objects in that cycle.
Would it be accurate to describe this as an asymmetry between safety and progress?

Yes. The prohibition on reclaiming protected reachable objects applies during crashes, partitions, and migration. The 3-round reclamation deadline applies to unreachable cycles after recovery and quiescence. Those are different conditions; the deadline does not relax safety before or after it begins.
I want to make sure the number is read correctly. Is this a three-second bound?

No. The stated measure is 3 collection rounds, not seconds or another elapsed-time unit. A design would need a clear account of what constitutes a collection round to demonstrate that bound, but the goal does not supply a round duration.
Does 'without global pauses' permit stopping the entire system briefly once recovery finishes?

Not as a way of meeting this requirement. Reclamation of the unreachable cycles must meet the 3-collection-round bound without global pauses. The goal does not prescribe a particular alternative mechanism; it rules out relying on a system-wide pause.
Could a proposed design claim success if it never frees anything that might be referenced?

It could claim the safety half only if it truly never reclaims an object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference. It would still fail the other half if unreachable cycles were not reclaimed within 3 collection rounds after recovery and quiescence.
What should I check when reviewing a design, without assuming any particular protocol?

Check each guarantee against its stated conditions. For safety, ask whether a reachable object can be mistaken for garbage while a reference is in flight, an object is migrating, communication is partitioned, or a participant is crashing or recovering. For progress, ask whether a genuinely unreachable cycle is reclaimed within 3 collection rounds once recovery and quiescence hold. Finally, check that the claimed progress does not depend on a global pause.
Should I treat a lack of replies during a partition as proof that an object has no incoming references?

No. Lack of replies does not establish that a durable root or in-flight reference cannot reach the object. The safety requirement is about actual reachability, not just the references currently visible to one participant.
Then the core challenge is to avoid premature reclamation under uncertainty while still making bounded progress once the uncertainty is resolved?

That captures the tension, with the precise bound kept in view: safely reclaim unreachable cycles within 3 collection rounds after recovery and quiescence, and do so without global pauses. Throughout crashes, partitions, and concurrent migration, no object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference may be reclaimed.
For the collector design, I propose durable reference and message logs, atomic migration handoffs, and concurrent epoch tracing. It would sweep unmarked cycles after two fully acknowledged rounds.

That proposal addresses the main sources of uncertainty in the goal. Durable reference and message logs are intended to preserve an account of references across crashes and message transit. Atomic migration handoffs are intended to keep migration from creating a gap in that account. Concurrent epoch tracing provides a way to assess reachability without a global pause. The proposed sweep rule is deliberately conditional: an unmarked cycle is swept after two fully acknowledged rounds, not merely after two rounds have been started.
Why include message logs as well as reference logs?

The safety requirement covers in-flight references, not only references already represented at an object’s current location. A message carrying a reference can be relevant to reachability while it is in transit. The proposal uses durable message logs alongside durable reference logs so that such references are not simply overlooked when communication is delayed or a crash occurs.
Is the word 'durable' important for both logs?

Yes. Crash recovery is part of the setting, so a record that disappears with a crash could not, by itself, support the intended accounting across that crash. The proposal specifically calls for durable reference and message logs. It does not yet specify their record format or the procedure for recovering from them.
What is the atomic migration handoff meant to prevent?

It is meant to prevent migration from creating an apparent interval in which an object, or references relevant to it, fall out of the collector’s view merely because responsibility is moving. Calling the handoff atomic states the intended indivisibility of that transition; the proposal does not spell out the handoff protocol.
So the collector should not interpret 'I no longer see it here' as 'it is unreachable' during migration?
Correct. Movement is not evidence of garbage. The proposed atomic handoff is one part of maintaining a coherent reachability account while migration and collection run concurrently.
Why use epoch tracing rather than stop everything to trace?

The goal requires reclamation without global pauses. Concurrent epoch tracing is the proposed approach for tracing while activity continues. Its correctness still depends on how the design accounts for references and changes that overlap a tracing epoch; naming epoch tracing alone does not resolve every concurrency case.
And why require two fully acknowledged rounds before sweeping an unmarked cycle?

That is the proposal’s reclamation threshold. It does not authorize sweeping simply because a cycle appears unmarked in a partial round. Both rounds must be fully acknowledged before the proposed sweep of an unmarked cycle. The node does not define who must acknowledge a round or what an acknowledgment certifies, so those details would have to be made precise to assess the safety argument.
If a partition prevents acknowledgments, does the proposal say to sweep anyway after two attempted rounds?

No. 'Two fully acknowledged rounds' is stronger than two attempted rounds. A partition that prevents the required acknowledgment cannot be treated as though a round were fully acknowledged. That distinction matters because lack of communication cannot establish that no in-flight reference reaches the cycle.
Does that conflict with reclaiming unreachable cycles within 3 collection rounds?

The progress requirement starts after recovery and quiescence. The proposed sweep threshold is after two fully acknowledged rounds, which is numerically within 3 collection rounds if those rounds can be completed and the cycle is identified as unmarked. That comparison is not, on its own, a proof of the 3-round guarantee: the design would still need to show when tracing identifies an unreachable cycle, what counts as a completed round, and when sweeping takes effect.
So 'two' is a proposed sweep condition, not a claim that all cycles have already been reclaimed in two rounds?

Exactly. The proposal says to sweep unmarked cycles after two fully acknowledged rounds. It does not state that every unreachable cycle is necessarily marked or classified in a particular way by a specified point, nor does it provide a completed proof of the broader deadline.
What should remain true if a crash happens while those rounds are under way?

The original safety condition remains in force: no object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference may be reclaimed because of the crash. The durable logs and the requirement for fully acknowledged rounds are proposed safeguards against mistaking incomplete observations for proof of unreachability. How a round interrupted by a crash is acknowledged or resumed is not specified here.
Is an unmarked cycle automatically garbage under this proposal?

Not merely because it is unmarked at some instant. The proposed rule requires two fully acknowledged rounds before sweeping an unmarked cycle. More fundamentally, the design must ensure that marking and acknowledgment adequately account for durable roots, in-flight references, crashes, partitions, and migration; otherwise an unmarked reachable cycle would be a safety failure.
Can I describe the three mechanisms as serving different parts of the same argument?

Yes, as a description of the proposal rather than an established proof. Durable reference and message logs address persistence of reference information; atomic handoffs address continuity during migration; concurrent epoch tracing addresses reachability assessment without global pauses. The two-fully-acknowledged-round condition governs when an unmarked cycle may be swept. Their interactions would need to support both the never-reclaim safety condition and the post-recovery, post-quiescence 3-round progress condition.
What is the most careful way to state the proposed reclamation rule?

Sweep an unmarked cycle only after two fully acknowledged collection rounds. Keep the qualification 'fully acknowledged': it is not interchangeable with two elapsed rounds, two initiated rounds, or two rounds with missing participants. And present it as the proposed rule, not as a demonstrated guarantee of safe reclamation.
How can an epoch close without overlooking references in unacknowledged messages or migration handoffs across a partition?

That is the key question for the proposed epoch tracing. An unacknowledged message might carry a reference, and an incomplete migration handoff might leave responsibility for an object uncertain. A partition makes silence especially ambiguous. Before a closed epoch can justify sweeping, its closure must mean that those references were accounted for or that any remaining uncertainty prevents the affected objects from being reclaimed. The proposal does not yet define how it establishes that.
Isn't the message log enough to account for an unacknowledged message?

A durable message log can preserve evidence that a reference-bearing message exists, including across a crash. But the log's presence alone does not explain what an epoch acknowledgment means or when a logged reference may cease to count. The closure rule must not overlook that reference just because delivery has not been acknowledged.
If the sender has recorded the message, can the collector treat the recipient's silence as harmless?

Only if the collector's reachability account still protects the reference despite that silence. An absent reply does not show that the message was delivered, that its reference disappeared, or that its target is unreachable. The unresolved part cannot be converted into evidence for reclamation.
What about an atomic migration handoff? Wouldn't atomicity settle the question?

Atomicity expresses the intended continuity of the handoff, but the question is how a collector recognizes that continuity when the parties are separated by a partition. It must not infer from one side's incomplete view that the object or a relevant reference has vanished. The proposal names atomic handoffs without specifying what an epoch can safely conclude about a handoff it cannot confirm.
So is it impossible to close any epoch while a partition exists?

That depends on what 'close' means. An epoch could be declared complete for some limited accounting purpose without authorizing reclamation of objects affected by unresolved references. But if closing an epoch is meant to certify that its unmarked objects can contribute to the two-fully-acknowledged-round sweep rule, a partition cannot simply be ignored. The question calls for a precise definition of closure and acknowledgment, not an automatic yes or no for every kind of epoch.
Could I count a round as fully acknowledged by the participants I can currently reach?

Not without establishing that this limited set of acknowledgments is sufficient to cover the references and handoffs relevant to the proposed sweep. Across a partition, a reachable subset's replies do not, by themselves, account for unacknowledged messages or migration on the other side. Calling such a round 'fully acknowledged' would need a justification consistent with the safety requirement.
Is the distinction between closing an epoch and authorizing a sweep important here?

Yes. A system might use the word 'closed' for an administrative boundary, while the reclamation decision requires a stronger claim about reachability. If those meanings are conflated, an epoch could appear finished even though an in-flight reference or migration handoff remains unresolved. The proposed two-round threshold is useful only if the acknowledgments have the meaning needed for safe sweeping.
Suppose an object is unmarked in both rounds, but a reference to it is in an unacknowledged message throughout. Does two rounds make it safe to sweep?

No. Two rounds of incomplete accounting do not erase an in-flight reference. If that reference makes the object reachable, reclaiming it would violate the safety requirement regardless of how many times it appeared unmarked. The issue is whether the rounds were fully acknowledged in a sense that includes or safely preserves that reference.
And the same reasoning applies if the uncertain item is a migration handoff instead of a message?

Yes. Repeated observations that omit an object during migration cannot establish unreachability if the handoff leaves its status unresolved. An epoch closure used for sweeping must not turn that uncertainty into a false negative in tracing.
Am I asking for an exact point at which uncertainty stops mattering?

In part. You are asking what evidence makes epoch closure safe when messages lack acknowledgments or handoffs span a partition. The answer has to distinguish a reference that remains protected from one that has been conclusively accounted for in the collector's reachability assessment. No such evidence rule is specified in the proposal as stated.
Would durable logs by themselves prove that all the relevant parties agree about an epoch?

No. Durability addresses survival of records; agreement or acknowledgment is a separate question. A record can survive a crash while a partition still prevents the collector from learning the status needed to make a sweeping decision. The closure rule has to connect persistent records, in-flight references, migration handoffs, and the meaning of acknowledgment.
Does delaying a sweep because of an unresolved partition undermine the three-round reclamation goal?

The 3-collection-round bound is stated for unreachable cycles after recovery and quiescence. It does not require unsafe sweeping while a partition leaves relevant information unresolved. It does require the design to make bounded progress once those conditions hold, so the treatment of unresolved epochs cannot become an indefinite obstacle after recovery and quiescence.
What should the question demand from a more precise design, without assuming its answer?

It should demand a definition of when an epoch is considered closed, what a full acknowledgment certifies, and how unacknowledged messages and migration handoffs remain represented across a partition. It should also ask why those definitions rule out sweeping an object reachable through an in-flight reference. Those are obligations for the proposed design, not details already established by naming logs, handoffs, and epoch tracing.
So if a partitioned participant cannot acknowledge, I shouldn't quietly treat the absence of an acknowledgment as an acknowledgment?

Exactly. Silence across a partition is uncertainty, not confirmation. Whether an epoch can close in some narrower sense is a separate matter; it cannot safely justify reclaiming affected objects merely by overlooking the unacknowledged message or migration handoff.

Here's a hypothesis for closing epochs: wait for durable message and migration acknowledgments. That should prevent false reclamation during a partition and still clear quiescent unreachable cycles within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence.

That directly addresses the uncertainty in unacknowledged messages and migration handoffs. Under the hypothesis, an epoch would not close on the strength of silence across a partition: it would wait for the relevant durable acknowledgments. The proposed safety and progress consequences are still hypotheses to establish, not results that follow merely from naming an acknowledgment rule.
Why insist that the acknowledgments themselves be durable?

If an acknowledgment is what permits an epoch to close, losing it during a crash could leave the collector without a reliable account of why closure was allowed. Requiring durable message and migration acknowledgments is intended to make that evidence survive crash recovery. The hypothesis does not specify how an acknowledgment is recorded or verified.
What exactly would a message acknowledgment need to settle?

For this hypothesis, it would need to settle the uncertainty relevant to a reference in the message before epoch closure relies on it. Merely observing that a message was sent, or receiving no response, is not the same as having the durable message acknowledgment the hypothesis requires. The precise meaning of that acknowledgment remains to be defined.
And a migration acknowledgment concerns the handoff rather than message delivery?

Yes. The hypothesis names both because an unacknowledged migration handoff can leave an object's status uncertain even if ordinary messages are accounted for. Epoch closure would wait for durable acknowledgment of that handoff as well. It does not specify the handoff's mechanics or which party supplies the acknowledgment.
If a partition blocks one of those acknowledgments, is the intended behavior simply not to close the affected epoch?

That is the proposed rule: closure waits for the durable message and migration acknowledgments it needs. A partition must not turn their absence into apparent proof that a reference or migrating object is gone. Waiting may delay reclamation during the partition, but avoids using an incomplete epoch to justify a false reclamation.
Does this make partition-time safety automatic?

Not automatically. The hypothesis is that waiting prevents partition-time false reclamation. To establish it, the design would have to show that every message or migration handoff whose reference matters to a reclamation decision is covered by the acknowledgment requirement, and that no sweep can bypass an epoch that has not safely closed.
Suppose a reference is still in an unacknowledged message when tracing finds its target unmarked. How should I interpret that observation?

As insufficient for reclaiming the target. Under the hypothesis, the missing durable message acknowledgment keeps the relevant epoch from closing for that decision. An unmarked observation cannot override the requirement never to reclaim an object reachable through an in-flight reference.
What if the uncertainty comes from migration instead?

The same proposed restraint applies: without the needed durable migration acknowledgment, epoch closure waits. An object must not be reclaimed just because concurrent migration made it temporarily absent from the collector's observed location.
Does waiting for acknowledgments imply a global pause?

Not by itself. Waiting to close an epoch is different from stopping all application activity. The hypothesis is framed alongside concurrent collection and the requirement to avoid global pauses. It still needs an account of how tracing and acknowledgment can proceed concurrently; the word 'waits' alone neither establishes nor requires a system-wide stop.
How can the hypothesis also claim to clear cycles within three rounds if an epoch can wait?

The timing claim is conditional. It concerns quiescent unreachable cycles after recovery and quiescence, not cycles while a partition continues to block needed acknowledgments. The hypothesis is that once those conditions hold, the needed durable acknowledgments and epoch closures allow reclamation within three collection rounds. That bounded-progress part needs its own argument; safety through waiting does not prove it.
Should I say 'three rounds' or 'two rounds' when stating this hypothesis?

State the hypothesis as clearing quiescent cycles within three collection rounds. The proposed sweep condition is after two fully acknowledged rounds, but the hypothesis makes a broader within-three-round claim after recovery and quiescence. Those numbers describe different parts of the proposed behavior and should not be substituted for one another.
Does an acknowledgment received after a partition heals retroactively make an earlier incomplete round fully acknowledged?

The hypothesis does not define that. It says epoch closure waits for durable message and migration acknowledgments. A precise design would have to explain how an acknowledgment relates to a particular epoch and collection round before making that inference. What matters here is not to treat the missing acknowledgment as present during the partition.
Could an acknowledgment be durable yet still fail to protect an in-flight reference?

Potentially, if its meaning were too weak or it did not cover the relevant reference. Durability says the acknowledgment persists; it does not by itself say what has been acknowledged. The proposed protection depends on both persistence and a meaning strong enough to make epoch closure safe.
Does the same distinction apply to migration acknowledgments?

Yes. A durable acknowledgment is useful only if it establishes what the collector needs to know about the migration handoff. Otherwise, persisting an ambiguous acknowledgment would not resolve the risk of overlooking a reachable object. The hypothesis identifies the needed category of evidence but leaves its exact semantics open.
Is the progress claim about every object that happens to look unmarked after recovery?

No. It is about clearing quiescent unreachable cycles within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence. Looking unmarked is not equivalent to being unreachable, especially if a reference or handoff is unresolved. The safety requirement still forbids reclaiming an object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference.
What if durable acknowledgments are delayed even after activity becomes quiescent?

That is a pressure point for the hypothesis. To meet the within-three-round claim, the design would have to show that the acknowledgments and closures needed for an unreachable cycle do not remain outstanding beyond that bound after recovery and quiescence. The hypothesis asserts the outcome but does not provide that demonstration.
So there are really two things to test in this idea?

Yes. First, whether waiting for durable message and migration acknowledgments truly prevents false reclamation across a partition, including for in-flight references and migrating objects. Second, whether the same closure rule still permits quiescent unreachable cycles to be cleared within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence, without global pauses. Neither consequence should be treated as established solely by stating the hypothesis.
I want to model-check CrashPartition-500 migration, delayed-acknowledgment, and crash-recovery schedules for reference safety and three-round cycle reclamation after quiescence.

That would evaluate both sides of the proposed collector behavior. The safety check asks whether any schedule permits reclamation of an object still reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference. The progress check asks whether an unreachable cycle is reclaimed within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence. Migration, delayed acknowledgments, and crash recovery are important schedules to examine because they can make the collector's view of references incomplete or temporarily uncertain. No model-checking outcome has been stated yet.
How should I phrase the safety property for this activity?

As an invariant: at no point may the collector reclaim an object that is reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference. Check it across the modeled CrashPartition-500 migration, delayed-acknowledgment, and crash-recovery schedules, including times when a partition or migration makes information unavailable. An object merely appearing unmarked is not enough to weaken that invariant.
Should the three-round check run from the start of a crash or partition?

No. The stated reclamation bound begins after recovery and quiescence. The model check should preserve that starting condition rather than count three rounds from the onset of a crash, partition, or migration. Safety, by contrast, must continue to hold while those events are in progress.
What precisely is being reclaimed under the progress check?

Unreachable cycles. The check is not that every unmarked object can be reclaimed, or that all collection work ends within three rounds. It is whether cycles that are actually unreachable are reclaimed within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence, without relying on a global pause.
How do delayed acknowledgments bear on the check?

They probe whether an epoch can be treated as closed, or an unmarked cycle swept, while a message or migration handoff still lacks the durable acknowledgment on which closure is supposed to wait. They also matter to progress: after recovery and quiescence, the modeled acknowledgment behavior must allow the proposed three-round reclamation claim to be assessed. A delayed acknowledgment must not silently be treated as an acknowledgment already received.
Is checking acknowledgment delays mainly a safety test, then?

It tests both properties. For safety, a delay must not create a false basis for reclaiming an object reached by an in-flight reference or affected by migration. For progress, the collector must not remain unable to reclaim an unreachable cycle beyond the three-round bound once recovery and quiescence hold. The two checks ask different questions about the same schedules.
What does migration add that a delayed message alone might not show?

Migration raises the handoff question: while an object is moving, does the collector maintain the reachability account needed to avoid premature reclamation? The model-checking activity includes migration schedules so that safety is checked while handoffs and tracing overlap. It does not assume that a message acknowledgment and a migration acknowledgment settle the same uncertainty.
And why include crash-recovery schedules rather than just partition schedules?

The goal requires safety through crashes and recovery as well as partitions. Crash-recovery schedules let the check ask whether the information relied on for reference safety and epoch closure remains adequate when execution is interrupted and resumes. They also provide the recovery condition from which the three-round progress requirement can eventually apply, once quiescence holds.
Does the name CrashPartition-500 specify how many crashes or participants are involved?

No such interpretation is provided. CrashPartition-500 is the specified name for this model-checking activity; the text does not define what the number 500 measures. It would be inappropriate to infer a participant count, crash count, or timing bound from the name alone.
When I inspect a model-checking outcome, what would count as a safety counterexample?

A schedule that reaches a reclamation while the reclaimed object is still reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference would be a safety counterexample. The relevant question is actual protected reachability at reclamation, not whether the collector happened to see a mark or receive a reply. This describes what to look for, not a counterexample that has been found.
What would a progress counterexample look like?

It would be an eligible execution in which recovery and quiescence hold, an unreachable cycle remains, and the cycle is not reclaimed within the following three collection rounds. Eligibility matters: a schedule still partitioned or not yet quiescent cannot be used to claim that the post-recovery, post-quiescence deadline was missed.
Could the checker just assert that two fully acknowledged rounds have happened and then test a sweep?

That could examine the proposed sweep condition, but it would not by itself establish the broader three-round reclamation requirement. The check also needs to determine whether an unreachable cycle reaches the point where it can be swept within the allowed rounds after recovery and quiescence. And for safety, 'fully acknowledged' must mean more than a label applied while relevant messages or migration handoffs remain unaccounted for.
Would a successful check prove the design safe under every possible failure schedule?

A model-checking result would support claims about the model and schedules it actually covers. The activity as stated names CrashPartition-500 migration, delayed-acknowledgment, and crash-recovery schedules; it does not specify the model's scope or report a result. It would be too strong to infer a universal proof from the proposed activity alone.
So I should keep the test objective separate from the findings?

Yes. The activity is to model-check those named schedules for reference safety and reclamation of unreachable cycles within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence. Whether the checks pass, fail, or leave a question unresolved is not given here.
Can the model check focus only on cycle reclamation and ignore references that are in flight?

No. That would omit part of the explicit safety objective. A cycle can appear unreachable from the collector's current observations while an in-flight reference still reaches it. The activity needs to check that such an object is never reclaimed, including under the migration, delayed-acknowledgment, and crash-recovery schedules being examined.
And if a cycle is genuinely unreachable after recovery and quiescence, retaining it forever would still be a failure of the check?

Yes. Avoiding reclamation can protect safety, but the progress objective requires an unreachable cycle to be reclaimed within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence. The model-checking activity is meant to examine that deadline alongside the prohibition on false reclamation, not trade one away for the other.

CrashPartition-500 found a schedule where the receiver crashes before persisting a migration acknowledgment. Replay omits that acknowledgment, and an unreachable cycle remains retained past three quiescent collection rounds.

The reported sequence has three distinct parts: the receiver crashes before the migration acknowledgment is persisted; replay omits the acknowledgment; and an unreachable cycle remains retained past three quiescent rounds. The finding concerns delayed reclamation of that cycle. It does not report reclamation of a reachable object.
Why does the point of the receiver crash matter?

The crash occurs before the migration acknowledgment is persisted. That ordering matters because the reported replay does not include the acknowledgment. The finding does not say that a durable acknowledgment was recorded and then lost; it says the receiver crashed before persisting one.
Is 'replay omits the acknowledgment' the same as saying the migration never happened?

No. It states what is absent from replay: the migration acknowledgment. It does not establish whether the migration itself completed, partly completed, or was reversed. Those details are not given in the finding.
What can I conclude about the cycle itself?

It is identified as unreachable, yet it remains retained past three quiescent collection rounds in this schedule. Its internal structure, size, and location are not specified; the relevant observation is that it is an unreachable cycle that has not been reclaimed by that point.
Does 'past three quiescent rounds' mean the cycle was retained only while the receiver was crashed?

No. The reported retention extends past three rounds described as quiescent. The finding does not give an exact duration for the crash or a detailed round-by-round timeline, so it should not be reduced to retention solely during the crash.
Should I say the acknowledgment was delayed rather than omitted?

For this finding, 'omitted on replay' is more precise. A delayed acknowledgment might still appear later; the reported sequence specifically says the receiver crashes before persisting the migration acknowledgment and replay omits it. The finding does not state that a later acknowledgment arrives.
Does this show a false reclamation during a partition?

No false reclamation is reported here. The observed outcome is retention of an unreachable cycle, not reclamation of an object reached through a durable root or an in-flight reference. CrashPartition-500 is the named check, but this particular finding should not be described as a demonstrated partition-time safety failure.
Can I infer that all crash-recovery schedules retain cycles this long?
No. CrashPartition-500 found this schedule. The finding does not say that every receiver crash, migration, or replay produces the same outcome.
Does the report tell us why replay omits the acknowledgment?

It gives the pertinent ordering: the receiver crashes before persisting the migration acknowledgment, and replay omits it. It does not specify the replay procedure or any additional reason for the omission.
What is the safest concise way to describe the finding without adding a diagnosis?

You could say: 'CrashPartition-500 found a receiver crash before persistence of a migration acknowledgment; replay omits the acknowledgment, and an unreachable cycle remains retained past three quiescent collection rounds.' That preserves the observed ordering and outcome without assuming additional protocol behavior.
Should I describe those as three rounds after recovery?

The finding says 'past three quiescent rounds.' It includes a crash and replay, but does not specify the exact point from which the rounds are counted relative to every stage of recovery. Keeping the reported wording avoids adding timing detail that is not supplied.
Does the result tell us whether durable message acknowledgments were also missing?
No. The omitted item identified here is a migration acknowledgment. The finding does not report the state of message acknowledgments or message logs.
Could I claim that the collector deliberately refused to close the epoch?

Not from this finding alone. The missing acknowledgment and the retained cycle are reported, but the trace as stated does not identify an epoch-closure decision or the collector's internal reason for retention. Calling that a deliberate refusal would add an implementation detail.
Is the receiver crash an observed schedule in the check, rather than a proposed failure scenario?

Yes. Here it is part of what CrashPartition-500 found: the receiver crashes before persisting the migration acknowledgment. The replay omission and retention past three quiescent rounds are reported as part of the same finding, not merely suggested possibilities.
How should I keep the safety and reclamation observations separate?

State the reclamation observation directly: an unreachable cycle remains retained past three quiescent collection rounds. Separately, note that this finding reports no reachable-object reclamation. That avoids turning a retention trace into a claim about safety outcomes the report does not provide.

I have a revised hypothesis for epoch closure: persist receipts and migration acceptance before exposure, then replay lost acknowledgments from receiver WALs. The aim is to reclaim quiescent unreachable cycles within three collection rounds.

That hypothesis puts a durable record ahead of exposure and uses receiver write-ahead logs, or WALs, to recover acknowledgments that are missing after a disruption. The intended effect is that an acknowledgment needed for epoch closure can be recovered without overlooking a reference or migration handoff. Reclamation within three rounds remains a claim to establish, not an observed result.
What does 'before exposure' contribute to the idea?

It specifies an ordering constraint: persist the relevant receipt or migration acceptance before the associated state is exposed. The hypothesis does not define the exact exposure boundary, so a full design would need to say what can become visible and to whom. The essential point here is that exposure must not precede the durable record intended to account for it.
Why mention receipts and migration acceptance separately?

They concern the two uncertainties in the epoch-closure question. A receipt is relevant to a received message, which may carry a reference. Migration acceptance is relevant to a handoff involving an object. The hypothesis requires persistence before exposure in both cases; it does not say that one kind of record can stand in for the other.
Are the receipts themselves the acknowledgments that get replayed?

The hypothesis does not specify an exact record format or equate the terms. It says to persist receipts and migration acceptance before exposure, and to replay lost acknowledgments from receiver WALs. The important proposed relationship is that the receiver's durable records provide the basis for recovering acknowledgments rather than treating their absence after a disruption as conclusive.
When we say an acknowledgment is 'lost,' does that mean its underlying event was never recorded?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis specifically relies on receiver WALs to replay lost acknowledgments, so it needs durable evidence from which an acknowledgment can be recovered. It should not be read as permission to invent an acknowledgment for a receipt or migration acceptance that was never persisted.
How does that help with a receiver crash?

The proposed ordering aims to leave a durable record before exposure, and the replay step aims to recover a missing acknowledgment from that record after a crash. Whether those steps cover every relevant crash point, and whether the recovered acknowledgment has the meaning needed for epoch closure, still require a precise account. A receiver crash alone must not turn an uncertain reference or handoff into evidence of unreachability.
What if the receiver crashes before it can persist the receipt or migration acceptance?

Under the proposed ordering, the corresponding exposure must not have happened before that persistence. But the hypothesis does not specify the full behavior of an interrupted receipt or handoff. An epoch could not safely manufacture the missing durable evidence or assume that uncertainty has been resolved merely because the receiver crashed.
Could replay close an epoch while the receiver remains across a network partition?

The hypothesis does not establish that a collector can access a receiver's WAL across an active partition. Replay of recoverable acknowledgments should not be confused with treating an unreachable receiver's silence as an acknowledgment. Any epoch closure used to justify reclamation still has to account for references in unacknowledged messages and unresolved migration handoffs.
So the WAL is not a substitute for actually resolving a partition?

Right. A WAL is intended to preserve evidence that can be used in recovery and replay; it does not, by its mere existence, make evidence available across a partition. The safety concern remains that an epoch must not close on an incomplete account of references.
Does recovering a lost acknowledgment prove that a particular object is unreachable?

No. It addresses a piece of uncertainty about message receipt or migration acceptance. Unreachability still depends on the reachability assessment, including durable roots and in-flight references. Replaying an acknowledgment can help establish what an epoch has accounted for; it is not itself a certificate that an object is garbage.
Then why connect acknowledgment replay to reclaiming cycles within three rounds?

The hypothesis is that recoverable acknowledgments prevent a missing acknowledgment from indefinitely blocking the collection of a quiescent unreachable cycle. To support the three-round claim, the design would need to show that recovery, replay, epoch closure, and reclamation fit within three collection rounds once recovery and quiescence hold. The proposed ordering and replay mechanism express a way that might happen, not a demonstrated bound.
Is the three-round clock running while a partition still prevents recovery?

No. The stated reclamation condition is after recovery and quiescence. Safety still applies during a partition, but the three-collection-round deadline for unreachable cycles is not a license to close an uncertain epoch while the partition persists.
Should 'quiescent cycles' mean cycles that have no internal references?

No. Cycles can have internal references; that is why cycle reclamation matters. In this hypothesis, the intended reclamation target is an unreachable cycle under the post-recovery, quiescent conditions. Quiescence does not by itself prove unreachability, and internal references do not by themselves make an otherwise unreachable cycle reachable from a durable root or an in-flight reference.
Could the collector replay acknowledgments and then immediately sweep everything unmarked?

The hypothesis does not authorize that. Replayed acknowledgments would need to have the correct relationship to epoch closure and tracing before any sweep could be justified. In particular, recovering an acknowledgment cannot excuse reclaiming an object still reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference.
Does persisting migration acceptance before exposure imply that migration has completed?

Not from the wording alone. It establishes an intended order for recording acceptance relative to exposure; it does not define every stage of migration or say that acceptance and completion are identical. A safe closure rule would have to use the acknowledgment's precise meaning rather than assume more than the record establishes.
What needs to be true about a replayed acknowledgment for epoch closure to rely on it?

It must correspond to durable receiver evidence relevant to the message or migration handoff whose uncertainty is being resolved. The closure rule would also need to identify which epoch or collection round that evidence can support. Otherwise, replay might restore an acknowledgment without establishing that the references relevant to a proposed reclamation have been accounted for.
Can I state the safety aim without claiming it has been proved?

Yes: the durable-before-exposure ordering and replay from receiver WALs are intended to let epoch closure account for messages and migration handoffs without treating missing acknowledgments as proof that their references disappeared. That is the safety rationale for the hypothesis, not a verified guarantee.
And how would you state the progress aim just as carefully?

The hypothesis is that replaying lost acknowledgments from receiver WALs allows quiescent unreachable cycles to be reclaimed within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence. The three-round limit and the conditional starting point are part of the claim; whether the mechanism actually meets it remains open.

Let's rerun CrashPartition-500, comparing volatile acknowledgments with WAL-persisted acknowledgments. I want to check epoch closure, reachable-object safety, and the number of collection rounds needed for reclamation after quiescence.

That sets up a comparison of acknowledgment persistence under the same named check. What exactly am I comparing when I say 'volatile versus WAL-persisted acknowledgments'?

You are comparing acknowledgments that are not persisted in the receiver WAL with acknowledgments backed by receiver WAL persistence. The activity does not specify other differences between the two cases.
Should I assume that WAL-persisted acknowledgments make epoch closure safe?

No. That is something the rerun is meant to examine. A durable record alone does not establish the full safety claim.
And should I expect volatile acknowledgments to fail?

The activity does not state an outcome for either case. Model-checking both lets you observe how acknowledgment persistence affects closure, safety, and reclamation rounds without assuming beforehand that either version passes or fails a particular property.

Examine whether a round is treated as closed when message or migration acknowledgments relevant to its reachability assessment remain unresolved. Could an epoch close even though an acknowledgment is still in transit?

That is one of the questions the rerun can probe. The activity does not predetermine how the modeled collector resolves that situation.
What does 'reachable-object safety' mean in the comparison?

It means checking that neither acknowledgment variant permits reclamation of an object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference. That safety condition continues to apply during crashes, partitions, and migration; it is not restricted to the period after quiescence.

It could show an absence of false reclamation in the schedules checked, but it would not settle the reclamation-round question. How do I avoid conflating an object's being unmarked with its being unreachable?

Keep the model's reachability property distinct from the collector's marking observation. For the safety check, ask whether an object that was reclaimed was actually reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference. For the progress check, identify genuinely unreachable cycles and count rounds to their reclamation. An unmarked observation alone settles neither question.
What starts the round count for the reclamation check?

The relevant condition is recovery and quiescence. Count collection rounds for an unreachable cycle under those conditions, rather than starting the three-round deadline while a partition, crash, or ongoing activity still prevents the stated starting conditions from holding.
Is 'within three rounds' the same as 'after two fully acknowledged rounds'?

No. Two fully acknowledged rounds is the proposed sweep threshold for unmarked cycles. Within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence is the broader reclamation requirement. The rerun can check both whether a sweep is authorized by the acknowledgments and whether the resulting reclamation occurs within the required number of rounds.
Should I report an epoch as closed just because tracing reached the end of a round?

Not without checking the acknowledgment condition that gives closure its meaning. Finishing tracing work and safely closing an epoch are not necessarily identical if relevant messages or migration handoffs are unresolved. The rerun is specifically checking epoch closure, so that distinction matters.
Why look at message and migration acknowledgments together rather than only migration acknowledgments?

Both can bear on whether a reference is accounted for. A message may carry an in-flight reference, while a migration handoff can make an object's status uncertain. Checking closure against only one category would leave the other source of uncertainty outside the stated safety question.
Does replay from a receiver WAL belong in the WAL-persisted case?

Yes, it is part of the proposed WAL-backed acknowledgment approach being evaluated. The activity does not report how replay behaves or whether it meets those checks.
Could the comparison focus solely on how fast the two variants close epochs?

No. Closure speed alone would miss reachable-object safety and the number of rounds until post-quiescence reclamation. A quick closure is not a success if it permits false reclamation, and a conservative closure is not sufficient if unreachable cycles remain beyond the three-round bound after recovery and quiescence.
How should partitions figure into the rerun?

CrashPartition-500 is the named check, and the closure question includes references in unacknowledged messages or migration handoffs across a partition. The rerun should not treat an absent acknowledgment during a partition as affirmative evidence that the corresponding reference is gone. If an object is reachable during a partition but becomes unreachable later, which property applies at each point?

While it is reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference, it must never be reclaimed, including during the partition. If a cycle is later genuinely unreachable and recovery and quiescence hold, the reclamation-round requirement becomes relevant. The comparison needs to preserve that distinction rather than use eventual unreachability to excuse earlier unsafe reclamation.

For each variant, report what the check finds about epoch closure, whether any reachable object is reclaimed, and the collection-round count for reclaiming eligible unreachable cycles after recovery and quiescence. Keep the volatile and WAL-persisted cases separate, and distinguish an observed result from a property that was merely intended or checked.
Can I already conclude that the WAL-persisted case meets the three-round target?

No. The current activity is to rerun CrashPartition-500 and check that target, not to announce its outcome. The WAL-persisted case must be assessed for safe epoch closure, reachable-object safety, and reclamation within three collection rounds after recovery and quiescence before any such conclusion can be drawn.

Yes. That keeps both the reported attribution and its scope: acknowledgment gating caused zero reachable-object deletions in CrashPartition-500. It would be broader to claim that gating prevents such deletions under every possible schedule.
What exactly did WAL replay retain?

Duplicate handoff records. The finding does not state how many duplicates there were, how they arose, or what fields they contained. It reports that they remained after WAL replay and delayed reclamation of the cycle.
Are duplicate handoff records evidence that two separate migrations occurred?
Not from this report. They are described as duplicate records, not as evidence of separate migrations. The finding does not give enough detail to reconstruct the underlying handoff events.
Does 'delaying reclamation to round four' mean the cycle was never reclaimed?
No. It says reclamation occurred in round four. The observation is a delay, not permanent retention.
Can I attribute that delay specifically to WAL replay retaining the duplicates?

Yes. That causal link is explicit in the finding: WAL replay retained duplicate handoff records, delaying cycle reclamation to round four. The report does not specify an additional mechanism between record retention and the delayed reclamation.

Since the rerun compared volatile and WAL-persisted acknowledgments, can I assign the zero-deletion result to each variant separately?

The finding does not give a separate zero-deletion count for each variant. Do we know whether the volatile case also reclaimed a cycle in round four?

Does the report say that an epoch closed prematurely?

Could I say the duplicate records were mistaken for live references?

That would add an explanation the report does not give. It attributes the delay to retained duplicate handoff records, but it does not say how the collector interpreted those records. It is safer to describe the retention and the round-four reclamation directly.
What about saying WAL replay introduced the duplicates?
The wording is narrower: WAL replay retained duplicate handoff records. It does not say whether replay created the duplicates or whether they were already present in the records being replayed.
Is the cycle identified as reachable at any point in this result?

No reachability history for that cycle is given. The result reports its reclamation in round four and separately reports zero reachable-object deletions. It does not describe the cycle's roots, references, or state in earlier rounds.
How should I distinguish the deletion observation from the reclamation timing in one sentence?

You could write: 'In CrashPartition-500, acknowledgment gating caused zero reachable-object deletions, while duplicate handoff records retained by WAL replay delayed cycle reclamation to round four.' That preserves both observations without adding a per-variant outcome or an unstated explanation of the duplicates.
Let's keep acknowledgment gates for safety. The decision is to persist receiver receipts and deduplicate handoff IDs, with the aim of eliminating crash-lost acknowledgments and fourth-round delays.

That keeps the safety restriction in place while addressing two sources of delayed reclamation. Persisting receiver receipts is intended to leave durable evidence when a crash interrupts acknowledgment. Deduplicating handoff IDs is intended to prevent repeated records for the same handoff from prolonging collection. Why keep the acknowledgment gates rather than loosen them to make reclamation faster?

The decision explicitly keeps them for safety. Faster epoch closure would not be acceptable if it meant treating an unacknowledged message or migration handoff as though it carried no relevant reference. The intended improvement is to make acknowledgments recoverable and avoid duplicate-handoff delays, not to remove the condition that protects reachable objects.
What does a persisted receiver receipt contribute if the acknowledgment itself is missing after a crash?

It is intended to provide durable receiver-side evidence of the receipt, rather than leave the collector dependent on an acknowledgment that may have been lost. The decision does not specify the exact recovery procedure or say that any missing acknowledgment can be recreated without such evidence.
Does persisting a receiver receipt mean the sender can assume delivery whenever the receiver is silent?

No. Silence during a crash or partition is not a persisted receipt. The acknowledgment gate remains: the collector must not treat the absence of a reply as evidence that an in-flight reference has disappeared.
How does deduplicating handoff IDs relate to the fourth-round delay?

The decision targets repeated records for a handoff as a source of delay. Deduplicating by handoff ID is meant to keep multiple records representing the same handoff from being counted as unresolved independent handoffs, thereby eliminating fourth-round delays of that kind. It remains an intended effect, not a demonstrated reclamation bound.
Could deduplication accidentally hide a real migration?

It must not. The intended distinction is between duplicate records bearing the same handoff ID and distinct handoffs. Deduplication cannot be allowed to discard information needed to account for a migration or a reachable object. This decision does not define the ID scheme or establish that its implementation is safe.
So are we choosing between safety and the three-round target?

No. Keeping acknowledgment gates preserves the safety constraint, while persisted receiver receipts and deduplicated handoff IDs are intended to remove obstacles to timely reclamation. The goal remains reclamation of unreachable cycles within 3 collection rounds after recovery and quiescence, without global pauses; this decision does not itself prove that bound.
Is 'eliminate crash-lost acknowledgments' a claim that crashes can no longer happen between any two steps?

No. It describes the problem the persisted receipts are meant to eliminate, not the disappearance of crashes or uncertainty. A crash can still occur; the point is to avoid permanently losing the receiver-side evidence needed to account for an acknowledgment. Whether the chosen persistence ordering accomplishes that for every relevant crash point remains to be established.
Should I describe the deduplication as a reason to skip an acknowledgment gate?

No. Deduplicating handoff IDs and retaining acknowledgment gates serve different purposes. Deduplication addresses repeated handoff records; gating still prevents an unresolved handoff or message from being treated as safely accounted for merely to advance collection.
What if two records share a handoff ID but there is still uncertainty about whether that handoff was accepted?

Removing the duplicate-record effect must not resolve an uncertainty that the records do not resolve. The gate should still require the acknowledgment evidence relevant to that handoff. Deduplication means not treating repeated records as separate handoffs; it does not turn an unacknowledged handoff into an acknowledged one.
Is receiver receipt persistence meant to replace the migration acknowledgment requirement?

The decision does not say to replace or drop acknowledgment gates. It calls for persisted receiver receipts while keeping those gates. The precise relationship among receipts, migration acceptance, and acknowledgments would need to be specified before asserting that a particular receipt satisfies a particular gate.
How should this behave during an unresolved network partition?

The decision does not authorize closing an uncertain epoch simply because a partition prevents replies. A durable receipt may provide evidence if it is available, but an unavailable or nonexistent receipt cannot be assumed. Keeping acknowledgment gates means unresolved messages and handoffs cannot be ignored to force reclamation during a partition.
And after recovery and quiescence, what is the intended benefit?

Persisted receiver receipts are intended to prevent a crash-lost acknowledgment from continuing to block progress, and deduplicated handoff IDs are intended to prevent repeated handoff records from causing a fourth-round delay. Together, they aim to permit timely reclamation while retaining the safety gates. The decision leaves verification of that outcome open.
Can I say the changes have fixed the fourth-round delay?
Not yet. You can say the decision is to deduplicate handoff IDs to eliminate fourth-round delays. Saying the delay has been eliminated would describe a result that this decision does not report.
What's the shortest faithful statement of the decision?

Keep acknowledgment gates for safety; persist receiver receipts and deduplicate handoff IDs to eliminate crash-lost acknowledgments and fourth-round delays. The latter are intended outcomes of the decision, not verified results.

I'd like to explore a distributed garbage-collection proposal using durable reference escrows and atomic migration handoffs. For cycles, it would use partition-fenced trial deletion to reclaim isolated cycles within three quiescent collection rounds.

That proposal combines reference protection with a way to reclaim cycles. Durable reference escrows are intended to keep references accounted for across failures; atomic migration handoffs are intended to preserve that accounting while objects move. Partition-fenced trial deletion is the proposed means of determining when an isolated cycle can be reclaimed without treating a partition's missing information as proof of unreachability. Reclamation within three quiescent rounds is the proposed bound, not an established result.
What does 'durable reference escrow' mean at the level this proposal actually specifies?

It names a durable way to account for references whose existence matters to reclamation. In particular, the collector must not lose track of a reference merely because of a crash or because communication is incomplete. The proposal does not specify an escrow record format, ownership rule, or release procedure, so those details should not be assumed.
Does an escrow make the reference itself a durable root?

Not necessarily. A durable root and an in-flight reference are both protected sources of reachability under the goal, but they are not interchangeable terms. The proposed escrow is a means of accounting for references; its presence should not be described as changing every reference into a root. What matters for safety is that no object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference is reclaimed.
Why pair escrows with atomic migration handoffs?

Collection and migration can overlap. An atomic handoff is intended to prevent the move from creating a gap in the reference or object accounting on which collection relies. The escrow addresses durable reference accounting; the handoff addresses continuity while an object migrates. The proposal does not say exactly how either is represented or coordinated.
If an object is absent from its old location during migration, can trial deletion take that as evidence that it is isolated?

No. Absence at a former location is not evidence that no durable root or in-flight reference can reach it. The proposed atomic handoff has to prevent migration from making a reachable object appear safely deletable. An isolation judgment would need to remain sound across the move.
What is trial deletion trying to establish for a cycle?

Conceptually, it tests whether a cycle's references to itself are the only reason its objects appear retained. Internal links can keep a cycle connected even when it is unreachable from protected sources. Trial deletion is useful only if the trial accounts for any references entering the cycle; otherwise an apparently isolated cycle could still be reachable.
So 'isolated' cannot just mean that the objects only refer to one another in the portion I can currently see?

Right. A partial view during a partition could miss an incoming reference. For this proposal to meet the safety goal, calling a cycle isolated must not overlook reachability through a durable root or an in-flight reference, including a reference whose status is obscured by migration or a partition. The proposal does not yet define the evidence required for that judgment.
What work does 'partition-fenced' do in the phrase 'partition-fenced trial deletion'?

It states the intended safety boundary around trial deletion in the presence of a partition. A partition must not allow a collector to treat an inaccessible source of references as though it held none. The proposal does not define the fence's mechanics or say precisely when it permits or blocks a deletion; those would be necessary parts of a full design.
Does that imply every trial must stop everywhere whenever any network partition occurs?

That does not follow from the wording. 'Partition-fenced' does not specify a system-wide stop, and the overall goal rules out global pauses as the way to achieve collection. What the proposal must establish is that no trial can reclaim a protected reachable object on the basis of information a partition has made incomplete.
Could the collector reclaim a cycle on one side of a partition if it looks isolated there?

The local appearance of isolation alone would not justify it. A reference from the other side, or one in flight, could still reach the cycle. Whether a partition-fenced trial could safely reclaim a particular cycle depends on what the fence establishes about those possibilities; the proposal has not specified that criterion.
Is the proposal promising to collect cycles during a continuing partition?

It does not expressly make that promise. It proposes partition-fenced trial deletion and reclamation of isolated cycles within three quiescent rounds. The broader progress goal is conditioned on recovery and quiescence, whereas safety continues through partitions. Neither condition should be replaced with a claim that collection must proceed despite unresolved partition uncertainty.
How should I read 'within three quiescent rounds'?

As a bound stated in collection rounds, under quiescent conditions, for reclaiming the isolated cycles addressed by the proposal. It is not a three-second deadline. The goal also calls for unreachable cycles to be reclaimed within 3 collection rounds after recovery and quiescence; showing that the proposed bound satisfies that goal would require clear definitions of a round, quiescence, isolation, and when reclamation occurs.
Does being quiescent by itself prove that a cycle is isolated?

No. Quiescence is a condition for assessing progress, not evidence that a particular cycle lacks incoming references. A cycle could remain reachable through a durable root even when activity has settled. The trial and its reference accounting still have to distinguish reachable cycles from isolated ones.
Could this proposal meet the time bound just by deleting every cycle on the third round?

No. The safety requirement does not expire on the third round. An object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference must never be reclaimed during crashes, partitions, or migration. The proposed three-quiescent-round bound applies to safe reclamation of isolated cycles, not indiscriminate deletion of cyclic structures.
Conversely, could the partition fence be so conservative that nothing is ever deleted?

That might avoid some unsafe reclamations, but it would not meet the proposed progress bound for isolated cycles or the goal's bound for unreachable cycles after recovery and quiescence. The design has to preserve safety under uncertainty and still make bounded progress when the conditions for reclamation hold.
What if a reference is in flight when a trial begins but arrives before the trial ends?

The trial cannot disregard that reference just because its status changes while collection runs. If it makes the cycle reachable, deleting the cycle would violate safety. The proposal's durable escrows, atomic handoffs, and partition fence are intended to support a sound account through concurrent changes, but the proposal does not specify a protocol for that particular timing.
And if migration overlaps trial deletion, neither side can assume the other has already accounted for the object?

That is the uncertainty an atomic handoff must address. A trial cannot use an apparent gap during migration as evidence of isolation. At the same time, the proposal would need to show that handoffs do not indefinitely obstruct reclamation of a genuinely isolated cycle once the stated quiescent conditions apply.
What would be the main obligations for evaluating this idea?

First, define what the durable escrows preserve about references across crashes and in-flight transfer. Second, define how an atomic migration handoff keeps reachability accounted for while an object moves. Third, state what the partition fence prevents a trial from concluding when information is unavailable. Then show that the trial never reclaims an object reachable through a durable root or an in-flight reference, and that eligible isolated cycles are reclaimed within three quiescent collection rounds without global pauses. Those are obligations of the proposal, not results already established.
How can trial deletion distinguish escrowed in-flight references from internal cycle edges when migration overlaps a partition?

That distinction is essential to a safe trial. An internal edge connects objects within the candidate cycle; an escrowed in-flight reference might enter that cycle from outside it. The latter can make the cycle reachable even if the collector cannot currently observe the reference's destination because migration and a partition overlap. The proposal does not yet specify what evidence lets trial deletion classify the two cases.
Why isn't it enough to look at the edges among the objects being tried?

Those edges show how the candidate objects refer to one another, but they do not rule out an incoming reference. Trial deletion must not mistake 'I see only internal edges' for 'only internal edges exist,' especially when a partition limits observation. An escrowed reference in flight could still reach an object in the candidate cycle.
Could the durable escrow itself establish that an in-flight reference is external?

It could be relevant evidence, but durability alone does not establish how the reference relates to a particular candidate cycle. To distinguish it from an internal edge, the trial needs a sound way to determine whether that escrowed reference can enter the candidate from outside. The proposal names durable reference escrows without defining their contents or how a trial interprets them.
If both kinds of reference ultimately point to the same object, why treat them differently?

Because their relationship to the candidate cycle differs. References entirely within an otherwise unreachable cycle do not, by themselves, make the cycle reachable from outside. A reference entering from a protected source can. The trial must preserve that distinction even when both references target an object in the cycle.
Does migration make it harder to decide which side of the candidate a reference comes from?

It can make the collector's observations harder to interpret while an object or its accounting is moving. A change of location must not be confused with a change in reachability. The question is how the trial maintains a reliable distinction between internal edges and escrowed in-flight references throughout the overlapping migration, rather than relying on a snapshot that may be incomplete.
And what specifically does the partition add to that uncertainty?

A partition can prevent the trial from obtaining information about a message or handoff when it needs it. An unanswered inquiry across the partition does not show that the reference is internal, absent, or no longer in flight. If the trial cannot resolve whether an escrowed reference enters the candidate cycle, it cannot safely use that uncertainty as evidence of isolation.
Would counting every escrow as an external edge be safe?

It could avoid deleting a cycle that an escrowed incoming reference reaches, but the question also concerns timely reclamation of cycles that really are isolated. If the trial cannot eventually distinguish relevant external references from references that do not keep the candidate reachable, it may retain unreachable cycles beyond the three-quiescent-round target. Conservatism alone does not settle both requirements.
Could I instead count every reference with a target inside the cycle as an internal edge?

No. A target inside the cycle does not make the reference internal; its source and reachability relationship matter. Treating an escrowed reference entering from outside as an internal edge could let trial deletion reclaim an object reachable through an in-flight reference, contrary to the safety requirement.
What if the reference was sent before the migration but arrives afterward?

Its timing cannot by itself make it safe to ignore. If it is an in-flight reference reaching the candidate, the collector must protect the reachable object across the migration. The question for trial deletion is how its accounting stays valid as the object's location changes, without assuming that arrival, handoff, or partition resolution occurred at an unstated point.
Does an atomic migration handoff automatically classify that reference for trial deletion?

Not automatically. An atomic handoff is meant to prevent a gap in accounting while an object moves, but the proposal has not specified how a trial reads handoff information or relates it to escrows and cycle edges. A sound classification still has to account for the reference when migration and a partition overlap.
Could the partition fence simply forbid every deletion until the partition ends?

That would avoid making a deletion based solely on missing information during the partition. But the wording 'partition-fenced trial deletion' does not specify that every deletion is forbidden, and the broader progress requirement applies after recovery and quiescence. The key obligation is to prevent an unresolved escrow or handoff from being misclassified as an internal edge while still enabling eligible unreachable cycles to be reclaimed within the stated bound.
Would it help to phrase the problem as determining whether there is any protected path into the candidate cycle?

Yes, provided 'protected path' includes reachability through durable roots and in-flight references. Internal edges can propagate reachability within a cycle, but they do not establish an incoming path by themselves. The difficult case in your question is an escrowed in-flight reference whose relationship to the candidate may be obscured by migration and a partition.
What would an incorrect trial-deletion conclusion look like?

One error would be to call the candidate isolated and reclaim it while an escrowed in-flight reference actually reaches it. The opposite problem would be to keep treating an unreachable candidate as possibly externally reachable after recovery and quiescence, so it is not reclaimed within three collection rounds. The question asks for a distinction reliable enough to avoid the first error without leaving the second unresolved indefinitely.
So can we answer the question with a definite classification rule yet?

Not from the proposal as stated. It identifies durable reference escrows, atomic migration handoffs, and partition-fenced trial deletion, but does not define the evidence or rule for classifying a particular escrowed reference against a candidate cycle. Any definite rule would need to show how it remains sound across the overlapping migration and partition and how it supports the three-quiescent-round reclamation bound.

Here's a hypothesis for trial deletion: generation-tagged durable escrows distinguish internal cycle edges from external references. Any unresolved external reference blocks deletion until reconciliation; after that, the cycle is reclaimed within three collection rounds.

That proposes a way to make the distinction the trial needs while preserving safety during uncertainty. The generation tags are intended to help identify internal cycle edges, while durable escrows keep relevant reference information available across failures. If an external reference remains unresolved, deletion waits for reconciliation rather than treating the uncertainty as evidence of isolation. Reclamation within three rounds after reconciliation is the hypothesis's progress claim, not yet an established result.
